bel_hall_guide.text: Welcome to City Hall. Portland stone outside, marble inside, and a copper dome that turned green ages ago.
Belfast became a city in 1888, and this building opened in 1906. It stands where the White Linen Hall once did.
Look up at the dome from inside. Then lie down, if the steward allows it. Nobody has ever managed to look bored.

then.text: Away and look at the dome. The yard built bigger, mind.

else.text: {greeting} Forty years at Harland and Wolff, man and boy. East Belfast born and bred.
I'm British, and Northern Irish, and proud of both. The Union isn't a flag to me. It's family, the yard, my da's medals.
The Troubles ran from the late sixties to '98. More than 3,500 dead. We lost a neighbour in the seventies, a good man. You don't forget.
The Agreement says we stay in the UK for as long as most people here want to. That's consent. I voted for it, and my brother didn't. We still do Sunday dinner.
Noted in the Gazetteer, under How these isles work.

then.text: Mind yourself. And read the plaques. Both sides wrote history here; the trick is reading all of it.

else.text: {greeting} I teach history up the Falls Road. In this city that's a bit like teaching weather to fishermen.
My mammy marched for civil rights in 1968. Fair housing, fair jobs, one man one vote. Then it all went bad, for everyone.
I'm Irish, and I'd like a united Ireland one day. The Agreement says that can happen, but only if people vote for it, North and South.
It was reached on Good Friday, 10 April 1998. 71% voted yes up here and 94% in the South. My class find that the hardest bit to believe: people agreeing.
Noted in the Gazetteer, under How these isles work.

then.text: Back to the library. The dissertation won't write itself. I've checked.

else.text: {greeting} Politics at Queen's. Ask me anything. Except about my dissertation.
I was born after the Agreement. It says people born here can be British, Irish or both, so I've both passports. Belt and braces.
In the 2021 census about a third here said British only, nearly as many said Irish only, and about one in five just Northern Irish.
The Assembly sits up at Stormont, 90 members. The First Minister and deputy First Minister share one office with equal power. So far one unionist, one nationalist.
If the parties can't agree, it stops. It's been down more than once. When it works it's slow. Slow beats the alternative.
Noted in the Gazetteer, under How these isles work.
